newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary's Horn floats idea of grand coalition.
newsitem.headline: Hungary's Horn floats idea of grand coalition.

text.p: Hungarian Prime Minister Gyula Horn, whose Socialist Party has slipped badly in opinion polls, called on Monday for an anti-extremist "grand coalition" in the run-up to NATO and EU membership after elections next year.
"There will be four or five parties represented in the next parliament and inter-party squabbling should be subordinated to the interests of the country," Horn told reporters.
Hungary is now governed by a strong two-party coalition made up of the Socialists, with 52 percent of all parliamentary seats, and the liberal Free Democrats, who have 20 percent.
But after two years of austerity policies which have seen real wages fall by more than 10 percent, both parties have lost much of their support.
They now trail two opposition parties, the conservative Smallholders and the Association of Young Democrats, in the polls.

"The coming four or five years will be very important because there will be decisions on joining NATO and the European Union," Horn said. "We should be open to each other and we should be aware of Hungary's image abroad."
Hw said he could envisage working with any party which declared itself against extremism but predicted the current centre-left coalition would lead the "national front".

"A future coalition depends on the parties' platform and their election results, but three years of successful centre-left government show that it should be the determining force in directing this process," he said.

Horn, whose own popularity is at an all-time low, is also coming under some pressure from inside the Socialist Party, whose social democratic wing last week called for personnel changes to deal with a lack of public confidence.

Despite not being named, Horn reacted angrily to the proposal, declaring that he would not allow a change of direction. "As long as I head the government, I shall not alter its policy," he said last week.

Asked on Monday whether he would adopt British former prime minister John Major's "put up or shut up" tactic of calling a snap leadership election to deal with criticism from within his party, Horn replied, "That's a good idea. I'll think about it."
In 1995, Major comfortably won a challenge to his leadership of the then governing Conservatives after calling an internal party election over repeated criticism of his performance.
